profileName: UkrHook — C2 Idiomatic Nuance, Systems Wit & Academic Polish (C+)

watchOuts.title: Trading 'Correct Textbook English' for Native Subtext & Color
watchOuts.detail: At C+, your grammar is airtight—the real edge lies in idiomatic economy and register shifts. Swap flat academic descriptors ('very complex', 'suddenly changed') for vivid, high-precision idioms ('a labyrinthine legacy codebase', 'moved the goalposts mid-sprint').

watchOuts.title: Zero-Article Generalizations vs. Specific System Instances
watchOuts.detail: Even near-native Ukrainian speakers occasionally slip on abstract vs. concrete article boundaries in fast technical debate ('the distributed consensus' in general → 'distributed consensus', vs. 'the consensus algorithm we shipped').

watchOuts.tag: Register Agility · CS Master's vs. Engineering Standup
watchOuts.title: Code-Switching Between Formal Thesis Prose and Dry Developer Wit
watchOuts.detail: Watch out for letting academic thesis phrasing ('furthermore, one must consider...') bleed into casual engineering banter, or vice versa. Master the pivot from dry, understated humor in standups to razor-sharp analytical prose in your defense.

watchOuts.title: Nuanced Phrasal Verbs That Carry Executive & Peer Punch
watchOuts.detail: Elevate standard Latinate verbs with native phrasal equivalents where punchiness counts: 'iron out' edge cases, 'boil down to' a core invariant, 'shoehorn' a feature into an architecture, or 'double down on' an optimization.

watchOuts.title: Deadpan Timing & Pitch Drop for Dry Humor
watchOuts.detail: Native-level wit relies on contrast and timing—delivering an absurd technical metaphor ('duct-taping a rocket booster onto a bicycle') with calm, unhurried downward inflection makes the punchline land effortlessly.

scenarios.title: Defending a Wild CS Master's Thesis Idea to a Skeptical Professor
scenarios.prompt: Pitch an unconventional computer science research angle over virtual coffee. Balance rigorous theoretical vocabulary with effortless, conversational idioms—turning a dense algorithmic trade-off into an engaging, crystal-clear story.

scenarios.title: World of Warcraft Guild Leadership as Distributed Systems Architecture
scenarios.prompt: Explain why coordinating a 25-player raid in WoW is the ultimate stress test for fault tolerance, latency, and human consensus protocols. Lean into vivid idioms, dry humor, and sharp technical metaphors.

scenarios.title: Rescuing a 'Curse-of-the-Legacy-Monolith' Sprint Without Losing Your Cool
scenarios.prompt: Tell an upbeat, entertaining story about untangling a bizarre production bug or architectural rabbit hole. Use at least three natural idioms (e.g., 'opened a can of worms', 'silver bullet', 'cut corners') without forcing them.

scenarios.title: The 'Rubber Duck' Debate: Will AI Replace Lead Architects or Just Create Better Bugs?
scenarios.prompt: Take a playful, nuanced stance on modern developer tooling. Practice hedging with C2 sophistication ('by and large', 'a double-edged sword', 'for all intents and purposes') while keeping the tone light and sharp.

scenarios.title: Designing the Ultimate Co-Op Strategy Game Over Late-Night Coffee
scenarios.prompt: Brainstorm the mechanics, economy, and lore of a dream game with a fellow designer. Focus on evocative descriptive vocabulary and natural conversational rhythm rather than rehearsed bullet points.

customCards.term: C2 Idiomatic Upgrade: "Fixing that one tiny bug unexpectedly revealed twenty deeper architectural problems."
customCards.definition: "Pulling on that one thread opened a whole can of worms in the legacy layer."
customCards.example: We thought it was a five-minute patch, only to realize we'd opened a massive can of worms.
customCards.note: Idiomatic Precision: 'Pulling on a thread' + 'can of worms' captures cascading technical debt with native economy.

customCards.term: Nuance Check: What is the difference between 'a silver bullet' and 'a double-edged sword' in tech architecture?
customCards.definition: 'A silver bullet' is a mythical one-size-fits-all cure; 'a double-edged sword' is a tool whose strengths carry equal risks.
customCards.example: Microservices are no silver bullet—for a small team, they're often a double-edged sword.
customCards.note: C2 Metaphor Control: Both idioms are staples of senior engineering debates; keep their distinct logic sharp.

customCards.term: C2 Academic Upgrade: "Even though the algorithm is slow in theory, in real life it works very well."
customCards.definition: "Notwithstanding its worst-case complexity, the algorithm holds up remarkably well in the wild."
customCards.example: In the wild, heuristic pruning beats theoretical worst-case bounds almost every time.
customCards.note: Register & Color: 'In the wild' bridges formal CS theory and real-world engineering effortlessly.

customCards.term: Idiom in Context: What does it mean when product leadership 'moves the goalposts' mid-sprint?
customCards.definition: Unfairly changing the acceptance criteria or definition of success after work is already underway.
customCards.example: Every time we're close to shipping, stakeholders move the goalposts on performance benchmarks.
customCards.note: Workplace Idiom: Crisp, diplomatic shorthand for shifting scope without sounding overly confrontational.

customCards.term: C2 Upgrade: "We forced a quick solution into the system even though it didn't really fit."
customCards.definition: "We shoehorned a hotfix into the pipeline to get through the release."
customCards.example: You can only shoehorn so many workarounds into a schema before it collapses under its own weight.
customCards.note: Vivid Verbs: 'Shoehorn' instantly paints the picture of forcing an ill-fitting piece into tight space.

customCards.term: Nuance Check: 'By and large' vs. 'For all intents and purposes' — how do their shades of meaning differ?
customCards.definition: 'By and large' = generally / on the whole (allowing minor exceptions); 'For all intents and purposes' = practically / in effect (even if not technically).
customCards.example: By and large, the migration went smoothly, and for all intents and purposes the old cluster is retired.
customCards.note: C2 Discourse Markers: Mastering subtle hedges separates near-native precision from textbook C1.

customCards.term: Playful Wit Upgrade: "That new framework looks impressive, but underneath it has no real substance."
customCards.definition: "That framework is all smoke and mirrors—great landing page, zero resilience under load."
customCards.example: Once you benchmark past the demo, half of these AI wrappers are pure smoke and mirrors.
customCards.note: Idiomatic Punch: 'Smoke and mirrors' delivers dry, memorable skepticism in four words.

customCards.term: Phasal Verb Upgrade: "Ultimately, distributed systems design reduces to a trade-off between consistency and availability."
customCards.definition: "At the end of the day, distributed systems design boils down to consistency versus availability."
customCards.example: Strip away the jargon, and the whole architectural debate boils down to latency budgets.
customCards.note: Natural Synthesis: 'Boils down to' distills complex Master's-level concepts into crisp conversational English.
